name: Autosomal Dominant Prognathism

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Clinical and Radiographic Criteria for Prognathism

criteria.description: Prominent forward positioning of the mandible relative to the maxilla
Positive family history consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance
Radiographic evidence of mandibular prognathism on cephalometric imaging
Lack of associated syndromic or systemic abnormalities

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of mandibular protrusion, positive family history, and confirmatory cephalometric imaging
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis is primarily clinical supported by imaging and family history; genetic testing may be supportive but is not routinely performed.

imaging: Cephalometric radiographs showing mandibular overgrowth and altered jaw relationships
genetic: Autosomal dominant inheritance pattern observed in family pedigrees
No specific gene mutation consistently identified
other: Clinical examination revealing mandibular prognathism and Class III malocclusion

distinguishingFeatures: Soft tissue swelling and enlargement of hands and feet
Systemic features including hypertension and diabetes

redFlags: Rapid progression of mandibular overgrowth beyond childhood
Presence of systemic symptoms such as endocrine abnormalities
Signs of temporomandibular joint ankylosis or severe dysfunction
references: Nieminen P. Genetic basis of mandibular prognathism. J Dent Res. 2009;88(7):585-593.
Proffit WR, Fields HW, Sarver DM. Contemporary Orthodontics. 6th ed. Elsevier; 2018.
